title: Many-to-many via junction tables; semi-joins (EXISTS); anti-joins (NOT IN NULL trap)
summary: A many-to-many relationship is a table of links. EXISTS asks "is there at least one?" without repeating rows, and NOT EXISTS asks "is there none?" safely, while NOT IN returns nothing once its subquery yields a NULL.

examples.title: The trace-link table: composite key, cascades, idempotent linking

annotations.note: The junction table needs no id of its own: the pair is the identity. The composite primary key forbids duplicate links, makes both columns NOT NULL and builds an index starting with requirement_id. Attributes of the link itself (who linked, when, which kind) go here too.
CASCADE on both sides: a link means nothing once either end is gone. Compare the RESTRICT on test runs in the foreign keys lesson, where the child was evidence.

A multicolumn B-tree is most efficient for conditions on its leading column, so the key index serves "tests of this requirement". The reverse question, "requirements of this test", gets its own index.
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (from the modifying-data module) skips the duplicate: INSERT 0 0. Linking becomes idempotent, so a retried API request doesn't fail.
Two joins walk the relationship: requirement to link to test case. Each requirement appears once per linked test; REQ-EXPORT has no links and drops out of the inner joins.
Deleting test 11 removes its links to both requirements in the same statement: (1, 11) and (2, 11) are gone.

examples.title: Semi-joins with EXISTS, and 'verified' as EXISTS plus NOT EXISTS

annotations.note: last_passed NULL means "never run". A nullable boolean has three states, and every query on it has to handle the third (line 33).
The join repeats a requirement once per link. SELECT DISTINCT would hide that, but it still builds every pair first, and it stops working the moment you also select a column from the link side.

EXISTS returns each requirement at most once and can stop at the first matching link. The select list inside is ignored; SELECT 1 is the convention. r.id IN (SELECT requirement_id FROM trace_links) is the same semi-join, and PG 18 plans both identically here.
"Every linked test passed" is written as "no linked test failed to pass", plus EXISTS so a requirement without tests isn't verified vacuously. REQ-RESET is out because test 12 never ran.
IS NOT TRUE counts NULL as not passed. With last_passed = false, test 12's NULL would match nothing and REQ-RESET would wrongly count as verified.

examples.title: The NOT IN NULL trap, and NOT EXISTS as the fix

annotations.note: A legitimate nullable foreign key: ad-hoc runs belong to no test case. Nothing about the schema hints at the trap below.
While the subquery returns only 10, 10 and 12, NOT IN is correct: Locked account (11) never ran.

The same query, after one NULL arrived: 11 NOT IN (10, 10, 12, NULL) is 11 <> 10 AND ... AND 11 <> NULL, which is NULL, and WHERE keeps only true. Every row fails the same way: no rows, no error, no warning.
The trap in isolation. Without the NULL the answer is true; with it, NULL.

NOT EXISTS asks whether a matching row exists, and the NULL row simply doesn't match. EXPLAIN shows it as an Anti Join; NOT IN can't be planned that way because of its NULL semantics and runs as a filter over a hashed SubPlan.

LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL is the same anti-join. Test a column that is never NULL in real rows (r.id, the primary key); testing a nullable column would also keep matched rows that happen to hold NULL there.

use_cases: Trace links between requirements and test cases, tags on articles, users in groups, products in categories
EXISTS: 'has at least one' filters, such as requirements with tests or customers with an open order
NOT EXISTS: coverage gaps, never-run tests, orphan detection, and 'all X satisfy Y' written as 'no X violates Y'
strengths: The junction table's composite primary key makes links unique and indexed, with no surrogate id
EXISTS never duplicates outer rows and may stop at the first match, unlike JOIN plus DISTINCT
NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe and is planned as an anti-join
weaknesses: Every many-to-many traversal costs two joins, and the reverse direction needs its own index
NOT IN (subquery) is only correct while the subquery can never yield NULL, and it is not planned as an anti-join
EXISTS can't return columns of the inner table; when you need them, you need a join or LATERAL

pitfalls.title: NOT IN over a nullable column
pitfalls.detail: One NULL in the subquery result makes NOT IN NULL for every row, and the query returns nothing. Use NOT EXISTS, which also plans better.
pitfalls.bad: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT test_case_id FROM test_runs)
pitfalls.good: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM test_runs r WHERE r.test_case_id = t.id)

pitfalls.title: JOIN plus DISTINCT for an existence question
pitfalls.detail: It builds every pair and then removes duplicates; EXISTS asks the actual question and returns each outer row once.

pitfalls.title: A junction table without a unique pair
pitfalls.detail: A surrogate id with no UNIQUE (requirement_id, test_case_id) lets the same link be inserted twice, and every count over links is then wrong. Make the pair the primary key or at least unique.

pitfalls.title: Checking a nullable column in LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
pitfalls.detail: WHERE r.test_case_id IS NULL can't tell 'no match' from 'matched a row whose column is NULL'. Check a NOT NULL column of the right side, usually its primary key.

quiz.q: test_runs.test_case_id contains one NULL. What does `SELECT ... FROM test_cases WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT test_case_id FROM test_runs)` return?
options: The test cases that never ran
quiz.why: For every row, x NOT IN (..., NULL) is either false or NULL, never true, so WHERE keeps nothing.

quiz.q: A requirement has five linked tests. How many times does it appear in `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM trace_links l WHERE l.requirement_id = r.id)`?
quiz.why: EXISTS is a semi-join: it only asks whether a match exists, so each outer row appears at most once.

quiz.q: What is the result of `SELECT 11 NOT IN (10, NULL)`?
quiz.why: 11 <> 10 is true, 11 <> NULL is NULL, and true AND NULL is NULL.

quiz.q: Why does the junction table use `PRIMARY KEY (requirement_id, test_case_id)`?
options: Every table needs an integer id
It forbids duplicate links and indexes lookups by requirement
quiz.why: The pair is the link's identity; the key enforces uniqueness and its index leads with requirement_id. Cascading comes from the foreign keys.

body:
## Concept

Relational tables have no "list of ids" column that the database can check. A
many-to-many relationship (a requirement is verified by many test cases, a test case
covers many requirements) is a table of its own with one row per link: a **junction**
table. Its primary key is the pair, and it has a foreign key to each side.

Two query shapes go with it. A **semi-join** returns rows of A that have at least one
match in B, each at most once: `EXISTS` or `IN (subquery)`. An **anti-join** returns rows
of A with no match in B: `NOT EXISTS`, or `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE b.key IS NULL`. `NOT IN`
looks like an anti-join and isn't one when NULLs are involved.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/JPA: `@ManyToMany` generates exactly this join table and hides it. Mapping it as
  its own entity is what lets you add attributes to the link.
- Go/TS: in code you would keep a slice or `Set` of ids on one side. In a table that is
  the comma-separated-list (or id array) anti-pattern: no foreign key can check it.
- JS: `EXISTS` is `tests.some(...)`, `NOT EXISTS` is `!tests.some(...)`, and the
  "verified" query is `tests.length > 0 && tests.every(t => t.lastPassed === true)`.
  `Array.prototype.includes` is two-valued, so JS has no equivalent of the NOT IN trap.

## Design notes

Prefer EXISTS and NOT EXISTS for "has any" and "has none" questions, and reserve joins
for when you need columns from both sides. Treat `NOT IN (subquery)` as a review
finding unless the column is declared NOT NULL; even then NOT EXISTS says the same thing
and is planned as an anti-join. `NOT IN` over a literal list (`status NOT IN ('done',
'dropped')`) is fine as long as no NULL can appear in the list.

Name the junction table after the relationship (`trace_links`) once the link has
meaning of its own, and give it the index for the reverse direction from the start.
